claim: 39 COVID-19 patients were recruited and followed up for a median of 12.5 days (1–35 days).
source: We recruited 39 patients who were followed up for a median of 12.5 days (1–35 days), among them 23 had died.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract with specific numbers of patients and follow-up duration.

claim: Among the 39 recruited COVID-19 patients, 23 had died.
source: We recruited 39 patients who were followed up for a median of 12.5 days (1–35 days), among them 23 had died.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract with specific mortality count.

claim: Neutrophils are major sources of oxidative stress in blood of COVID-19 patients.
source: Analyzing blood samples from patients and healthy individuals (n=11), we provide evidence that neutrophils are major sources of oxidative stress in blood and that hydrogen peroxide is highly accumulated in plasmas of non-survivors.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from blood sample analysis comparing patients and healthy controls.

claim: Hydrogen peroxide is highly accumulated in plasmas of non-survivors.
source: Analyzing blood samples from patients and healthy individuals (n=11), we provide evidence that neutrophils are major sources of oxidative stress in blood and that hydrogen peroxide is highly accumulated in plasmas of non-survivors.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of hydrogen peroxide in plasma samples.

claim: Non-survivors' HSA showed dramatically reduced protein packing order parameter.
source: Non-survivors' HSA showed dramatically reduced protein packing order parameter, faster SLFA correlational rotational time, and smaller S/W ratio (strong-binding/weak-binding sites within HSA), all reflecting remarkably fluid protein microenvironments.
evidence: Supported by EPR spectroscopy measurements on HSA from different patient groups.

claim: Non-survivors' HSA showed faster SLFA correlational rotational time.
source: Non-survivors' HSA showed dramatically reduced protein packing order parameter, faster SLFA correlational rotational time, and smaller S/W ratio (strong-binding/weak-binding sites within HSA), all reflecting remarkably fluid protein microenvironments.
evidence: Supported by EPR spectroscopy measurements on HSA from different patient groups.

claim: Non-survivors' HSA showed smaller S/W ratio (strong-binding/weak-binding sites within HSA).
source: Non-survivors' HSA showed dramatically reduced protein packing order parameter, faster SLFA correlational rotational time, and smaller S/W ratio (strong-binding/weak-binding sites within HSA), all reflecting remarkably fluid protein microenvironments.
evidence: Supported by EPR spectroscopy measurements on HSA from different patient groups.

claim: The transport function of HSA may be impaired in severe COVID-19 patients.
source: Following loading/unloading of 16-DSA, we show that the transport function of HSA may be impaired in severe patients.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from loading/unloading experiments with 16-DSA.

claim: Lower values of S/W ratio (≤0.15) significantly predicted in-hospital mortality with 81.8% (18/22) mortality vs. 18.2% (4/22) for S/W>0.15, p=0.023.
source: Stratified at the means, Kaplan–Meier survival analysis indicated that lower values of S/W ratio and accumulated H2O2 in plasma significantly predicted in-hospital mortality (S/W≤0.15, 81.8% (18/22) vs. S/W>0.15, 18.2% (4/22), p=0.023; plasma [H2O2]>8.6 μM, 65.2% (15/23) vs. 34.8% (8/23), p=0.043).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis with specific statistical values.

claim: Plasma H2O2 concentration >8.6 μM significantly predicted in-hospital mortality with 65.2% (15/23) mortality vs. 34.8% (8/23), p=0.043.
source: Stratified at the means, Kaplan–Meier survival analysis indicated that lower values of S/W ratio and accumulated H2O2 in plasma significantly predicted in-hospital mortality (S/W≤0.15, 81.8% (18/22) vs. S/W>0.15, 18.2% (4/22), p=0.023; plasma [H2O2]>8.6 μM, 65.2% (15/23) vs. 34.8% (8/23), p=0.043).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis with specific statistical values.

claim: A risk score derived as the ratio ((S/W)/[H2O2]) lower than 0.019 predicted mortality with 95.5% (21/22) accuracy vs. 4.5% (1/22), log-rank χ2=12.1, p=4.9×10−4.
source: When we combined these two parameters as the ratio ((S/W)/[H2O2]) to derive a risk score, the resultant risk score lower than the mean (<0.019) predicted mortality with high fidelity (95.5% (21/22) vs. 4.5% (1/22), log-rank χ2=12.1, p=4.9×10−4).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis combining two parameters with specific statistical values.

claim: There have been more than 135 million confirmed COVID-19 cases including around 3 million deaths worldwide according to the World Health Organization.
source: While writing this report, there have been more than 135 million confirmed cases including around 3 million deaths worldwide according to the World Health Organization Coronavirus Disease Dashboard (https://covid19.who.int/).
evidence: Cited from WHO Coronavirus Disease Dashboard.

claim: Approximately 50% of COVID-19 cases are reported to be in the 25–64 age group.
source: Although 50% of cases are reported to be in the 25–64 age group, the percentage of deaths increases dramatically with age, and approximately 75% of deaths are in those aged 65 years and above (COVID-19 Hospitalization and Death by Age | CDC).
evidence: Cited from CDC data on COVID-19 hospitalization and death by age.

claim: Approximately 75% of COVID-19 deaths are in those aged 65 years and above.
source: Although 50% of cases are reported to be in the 25–64 age group, the percentage of deaths increases dramatically with age, and approximately 75% of deaths are in those aged 65 years and above (COVID-19 Hospitalization and Death by Age | CDC).
evidence: Cited from CDC data on COVID-19 hospitalization and death by age.

claim: People in the 30–39 years age group are 4 times more likely to die from COVID-19 complications compared to the 18–29 years age group.
source: People in the age groups 30–39 years, 40–49 years, and 50–64 years are 4, 10, and 30 times more likely to die from COVID-19 complications compared to the 18–29 years age group.
evidence: Stated as comparative mortality risk data.

claim: People in the 40–49 years age group are 10 times more likely to die from COVID-19 complications compared to the 18–29 years age group.
source: People in the age groups 30–39 years, 40–49 years, and 50–64 years are 4, 10, and 30 times more likely to die from COVID-19 complications compared to the 18–29 years age group.
evidence: Stated as comparative mortality risk data.

claim: People in the 50–64 years age group are 30 times more likely to die from COVID-19 complications compared to the 18–29 years age group.
source: People in the age groups 30–39 years, 40–49 years, and 50–64 years are 4, 10, and 30 times more likely to die from COVID-19 complications compared to the 18–29 years age group.
evidence: Stated as comparative mortality risk data.

claim: HSA is the most abundant constituent of soluble proteins in the circulatory system.
source: Human serum albumin (HSA) is the most abundant constituent of soluble proteins in the circulatory system.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about HSA.

claim: HSA has been suggested and used as a diagnostic and prognostic marker of numerous diseases including ischemia, rheumatoid arthritis, cancer, and septic shock.
source: HSA has been suggested and used as a diagnostic and prognostic marker of numerous diseases and conditions including ischemia, rheumatoid arthritis, cancer, septic shock, among many others.
evidence: General statement about HSA's clinical utility based on established literature.

claim: HSA maintains blood/tissue osmotic balance.
source: In addition to its numerous physiological and pharmacological functions including the maintenance of blood/tissue osmotic balance (Singh-Zocchi et al., 1999), blood pH, metal cation transport and homeostasis (Bal et al., 2013; Stewart et al., 2003), nutrients and drug shuttling (Fujiwara and Amisaki, 2013; Wishart et al., 2018), and toxin neutralization (Ascenzi et al., 2006; Vorum and Honoré, 1996), HSA is suggested to be a major circulating antioxidant (Cha and Kim, 1996; Loban et al., 1997).
evidence: Cited from Singh-Zocchi et al., 1999.

claim: HSA is involved in blood pH maintenance.
source: In addition to its numerous physiological and pharmacological functions including the maintenance of blood/tissue osmotic balance (Singh-Zocchi et al., 1999), blood pH, metal cation transport and homeostasis (Bal et al., 2013; Stewart et al., 2003), nutrients and drug shuttling (Fujiwara and Amisaki, 2013; Wishart et al., 2018), and toxin neutralization (Ascenzi et al., 2006; Vorum and Honoré, 1996), HSA is suggested to be a major circulating antioxidant (Cha and Kim, 1996; Loban et al., 1997).
evidence: Stated as a known function of HSA.

claim: HSA is involved in metal cation transport and homeostasis.
source: In addition to its numerous physiological and pharmacological functions including the maintenance of blood/tissue osmotic balance (Singh-Zocchi et al., 1999), blood pH, metal cation transport and homeostasis (Bal et al., 2013; Stewart et al., 2003), nutrients and drug shuttling (Fujiwara and Amisaki, 2013; Wishart et al., 2018), and toxin neutralization (Ascenzi et al., 2006; Vorum and Honoré, 1996), HSA is suggested to be a major circulating antioxidant (Cha and Kim, 1996; Loban et al., 1997).
evidence: Cited from Bal et al., 2013 and Stewart et al., 2003.

claim: HSA is involved in nutrients and drug shuttling.
source: In addition to its numerous physiological and pharmacological functions including the maintenance of blood/tissue osmotic balance (Singh-Zocchi et al., 1999), blood pH, metal cation transport and homeostasis (Bal et al., 2013; Stewart et al., 2003), nutrients and drug shuttling (Fujiwara and Amisaki, 2013; Wishart et al., 2018), and toxin neutralization (Ascenzi et al., 2006; Vorum and Honoré, 1996), HSA is suggested to be a major circulating antioxidant (Cha and Kim, 1996; Loban et al., 1997).
evidence: Cited from Fujiwara and Amisaki, 2013 and Wishart et al., 2018.

claim: HSA is involved in toxin neutralization.
source: In addition to its numerous physiological and pharmacological functions including the maintenance of blood/tissue osmotic balance (Singh-Zocchi et al., 1999), blood pH, metal cation transport and homeostasis (Bal et al., 2013; Stewart et al., 2003), nutrients and drug shuttling (Fujiwara and Amisaki, 2013; Wishart et al., 2018), and toxin neutralization (Ascenzi et al., 2006; Vorum and Honoré, 1996), HSA is suggested to be a major circulating antioxidant (Cha and Kim, 1996; Loban et al., 1997).
evidence: Cited from Ascenzi et al., 2006 and Vorum and Honoré, 1996.

claim: HSA is suggested to be a major circulating antioxidant.
source: In addition to its numerous physiological and pharmacological functions including the maintenance of blood/tissue osmotic balance (Singh-Zocchi et al., 1999), blood pH, metal cation transport and homeostasis (Bal et al., 2013; Stewart et al., 2003), nutrients and drug shuttling (Fujiwara and Amisaki, 2013; Wishart et al., 2018), and toxin neutralization (Ascenzi et al., 2006; Vorum and Honoré, 1996), HSA is suggested to be a major circulating antioxidant (Cha and Kim, 1996; Loban et al., 1997).
evidence: Cited from Cha and Kim, 1996 and Loban et al., 1997.

claim: HSA can bind with a diverse array of drugs and toxins, controlling their bioavailability and pharmacologic effects.
source: HSA can remarkably bind with a diverse array of drugs and toxins thus controlling their bioavailability and pharmacologic effects (Fasano et al., 2005).
evidence: Cited from Fasano et al., 2005.

claim: More than 70% of the free radical-trapping capacity of serum was due to HSA.
source: It has been previously shown that more than 70% of the free radical-trapping capacity of serum was due to HSA (reviewed in Roche et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from a review by Roche et al., 2008.

claim: Inflammation enhances vascular permeability of various tissues to HSA to confer antioxidant beneficial effects against reactive species released by activated neutrophils.
source: Importantly, several reports indicated that inflammation enhances vascular permeability of various tissues to HSA apparently to confer antioxidant beneficial effects against reactive species released by activated neutrophils (Cross et al., 1994; Halliwell, 1988; Sitar et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from Cross et al., 1994; Halliwell, 1988; Sitar et al., 2013.

claim: Neutrophilia-mediated oxidative stress was implicated in COVID-19 pathology and speculated to exacerbate the inflammatory immune response eventually causing multi-organ failure and death.
source: Although currently without direct experimental evidence, neutrophilia-mediated oxidative stress was implicated in the COVID-19 pathology and speculated to exacerbate the inflammatory immune response eventually causing multi-organ failure and death (Laforge et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from Laforge et al., 2020, but noted as lacking direct experimental evidence.

claim: Albumin has at least seven different specific binding sites for long-chain fatty acids located in different domains within the protein.
source: Albumin has at least seven different specific binding sites for long-chain fatty acids located in different domains within the protein (Bhattacharya et al., 2000; Curry et al., 1999; Simard et al., 2006).
evidence: Cited from Bhattacharya et al., 2000; Curry et al., 1999; Simard et al., 2006.

claim: No clinical or demographic characteristic showed statistically significant difference between Sev-R and Sev-D groups when analyzed by Pearson's Chi-square test.
source: No clinical or demographic characteristic showed statistically significant difference between Sev-R and Sev-D groups when analyzed by Pearson's Chi-square test.
evidence: Statistical analysis of demographic and clinical data in Table 1.

claim: Albumin level showed a significant decrease in non-survivors compared to survivors (p<0.05).
source: Although when comparing all parameters in the two COVID-19 groups, we observed changes following the same reported trends in the literature, means' comparisons by Tukey test reported non-significant changes in all parameters except for a significant decrease in albumin level (p<0.05) and a strong trend observed for C-reactive protein (CRP) (greater levels in Sev-D group, p=0.06).
evidence: Statistical comparison of laboratory parameters between survivor and non-survivor groups.

claim: C-reactive protein (CRP) showed a strong trend toward greater levels in Sev-D group (p=0.06).
source: Although when comparing all parameters in the two COVID-19 groups, we observed changes following the same reported trends in the literature, means' comparisons by Tukey test reported non-significant changes in all parameters except for a significant decrease in albumin level (p<0.05) and a strong trend observed for C-reactive protein (CRP) (greater levels in Sev-D group, p=0.06).
evidence: Statistical comparison of laboratory parameters between survivor and non-survivor groups.

claim: Non-survivors' blood carried increased CRP, D-dimer, IL-6, ferritin, and liver enzymes ALT and AST.
source: Nevertheless, non-survivors' blood carried the frequently observed hallmarks of increased CRP, D-dimer, IL-6, ferritin, and the liver enzymes ALT and AST (reviewed in: Singh et al., 2021; Velavan and Meyer, 2020).
evidence: Cited from reviews by Singh et al., 2021 and Velavan and Meyer, 2020.

claim: Neutrophil counts significantly increased in the order Control (40.78±14.0) < Sev-R (64.0±20.0) < Sev-D (76.4±6.8) with overall ANOVA p=3.9×10–5.
source: Figure 2 shows that while lymphocyte counts decrease, a parallel dramatic increase in neutrophil counts (% total) was observable when going from Control (40.78±14.0, n=9) to Sev-R (64.0±20.0, n=10) to Sev-D (76.4± 6.8, n=11) groups (overall ANOVA p=3.9×10–5).
evidence: Flow cytometry data with statistical analysis.

claim: Neutrophil counts strongly correlated with DCF-positive neutrophil counts (Pearson's r=0.8, p=3×10–7).
source: To confirm this relation, we compared neutrophil counts with DCF-positive neutrophil counts and found that the two parameters were strongly correlated (Pearson's r=0.8, p=3×10–7; Figure 2C).
evidence: Correlation analysis of flow cytometry data.

claim: Both neutrophil counts and DCF-positive neutrophil counts showed statistically significant increases in both COVID-19 groups compared with the control group.
source: Moreover, both parameters individually showed statistically significant increases in both of the studied COVID-19 groups when compared with the control group (Figure 2D&E).
evidence: Flow cytometry data with statistical comparisons shown in Figure 2D&E.

claim: Plasma hydrogen peroxide levels were significantly different between groups: Control (2.95±0.77 μM), Sev-R (7.21±2.4 μM), Sev-D (9.67±2.0 μM) with overall ANOVA p=2.6×10–11.
source: Indeed, we detected striking differences between groups even with relatively small sample sizes (Mean ± SD, Control, n=11: 2.95±0.77, Sev-R, n=16: 7.21±2.4, Sev-D, n=23: 9.67±2.0; overall ANOVA p=2.6×10–11; Figure 3C).
evidence: Catalase-based assay measurements with statistical analysis.

claim: Plasma hydrogen peroxide levels in survivors were doubled relative to controls (Sev-R vs. Control, 95% CI: 2.37‒6.13, p=4.9×10–6).
source: The differences between groups have reached statistical significance (Sev-R vs. Control, 95% CI: 2.37‒6.13, p=4.9×10–6; Sev-D vs. Control, 95% CI: 4.95‒8.48, p=0.0; Sev-D vs. Sev-R, 95% CI: 0.90‒4.03, p=0.001).
evidence: Statistical comparison of hydrogen peroxide measurements.

claim: Plasma hydrogen peroxide levels in deceased patients were tripled relative to controls (Sev-D vs. Control, 95% CI: 4.95‒8.48, p=0.0).
source: The differences between groups have reached statistical significance (Sev-R vs. Control, 95% CI: 2.37‒6.13, p=4.9×10–6; Sev-D vs. Control, 95% CI: 4.95‒8.48, p=0.0; Sev-D vs. Sev-R, 95% CI: 0.90‒4.03, p=0.001).
evidence: Statistical comparison of hydrogen peroxide measurements.

claim: Plasma hydrogen peroxide levels were significantly higher in Sev-D compared to Sev-R (95% CI: 0.90‒4.03, p=0.001).
source: The differences between groups have reached statistical significance (Sev-R vs. Control, 95% CI: 2.37‒6.13, p=4.9×10–6; Sev-D vs. Control, 95% CI: 4.95‒8.48, p=0.0; Sev-D vs. Sev-R, 95% CI: 0.90‒4.03, p=0.001).
evidence: Statistical comparison of hydrogen peroxide measurements.

claim: Neutrophils from a survivor patient showed significantly reduced average neutrophil DNA area (36.0±7.5 μm2) compared to control (144.8±93.7 μm2) with p=0.
source: Although requiring more detailed studies, a closer look at the acquired images of Hoechst-stained neutrophils from a survivor patient showed significantly reduced average neutrophil size (control DNA area, 144.8±93.7 μm2 [133 cells analyzed] vs. Sev-R DNA area, 36.0±7.5 μm2 [241 cells analyzed], Welsh corrected two samples t-test, p=0) with tendencies toward more condensed, more segmented nuclei and frequent C-shaped chromatin.
evidence: Fluorescence imaging analysis of isolated neutrophils.

claim: Neutrophils from a non-survivor exhibited a 26% larger DNA area than normal cells and roughly five times that of Sev-R neutrophils (DNA area 182.7±171 μm2, p=0 vs. both control and Sev-R groups).
source: However, neutrophils from a non-survivor exhibited diffused chromatin and possessed in average, a 26% larger DNA area than normal cells and roughly five times that of Sev-R neutrophils (DNA area [97 cells analyzed], 182.7±171 μm2, p=0 vs. both control and Sev-R groups).
evidence: Fluorescence imaging analysis of isolated neutrophils.

claim: DCF mean fluorescence intensities per cell increased in the order Control (6.7±0.7×10³) < Sev-R (10.9±0.9×10³) < Sev-D (13.0±1.1×10³) with p=0 for all comparisons.
source: Analysis of mean DCF fluorescence intensities (MFI) per cell confirmed results obtained by flow cytometry and catalase assay reporting increased levels of ROS in the order control<< Sev-R<Sev-D (DCF MFI ± SD [×103]: Control [282 cells analyzed], 6.7±0.7; Sev-R [351 cells analyzed], 10.9±0.9; Sev-D [368 cells analyzed], 13.0±1.1, Welsh corrected two samples t-test, p=0 for all comparisons).
evidence: Fluorescence imaging analysis with statistical comparisons.

claim: Non-survivor COVID-19 patients exhibit mild but consistent hypoalbuminemia relative to survivors.
source: It has been previously shown that non-survivor COVID-19 patients exhibit mild but consistent hypoalbuminemia relative to survivors (Violi et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from Violi et al., 2020.

claim: Albumin concentration in plasma decreased in the order Control (40.45±10.93 mg/ml) > Sev-R (31.47±7.95 mg/ml) > Sev-D (26.97±5.10 mg/ml) with overall ANOVA p=2.4×10–4.
source: We found that [albumin] in plasma decreased in the order Control>Sev-R>Sev-D (Mean ± SD, Control, n=8: 40.45±10.93 mg/ml, Sev-R, n=16: 31.47±7.95 mg/ml, Sev-D, n=23: 26.97±5.10 mg/ml; overall ANOVA p=2.4×10–4; Figure 4A).
evidence: Albumin concentration measurements with statistical analysis.

claim: Albumin concentration was significantly decreased in Sev-R compared to Control (95% CI: –16.66 to –1.28, p=0.02).
source: We detected statistically significant decrease in [albumin] in plasma of Sev-R and Sev-D groups (Sev-R vs. Control, 95% CI: –16.66 to –1.28, p=0.02; Sev-D vs. Control, 95% CI: –20.76 to –6.18, p=1.5×10–4; Sev-D vs. Sev-D, 95% CI: –10.28 to 1.28, p=0.15).
evidence: Statistical comparison of albumin measurements.

claim: Albumin concentration was significantly decreased in Sev-D compared to Control (95% CI: –20.76 to –6.18, p=1.5×10–4).
source: We detected statistically significant decrease in [albumin] in plasma of Sev-R and Sev-D groups (Sev-R vs. Control, 95% CI: –16.66 to –1.28, p=0.02; Sev-D vs. Control, 95% CI: –20.76 to –6.18, p=1.5×10–4; Sev-D vs. Sev-D, 95% CI: –10.28 to 1.28, p=0.15).
evidence: Statistical comparison of albumin measurements.

claim: The reference range of HSA concentration in serum is approximately 35–50 mg/ml.
source: The reference range of HSA concentration in serum is approximately 35–50 mg/ml, but we and other groups found that COVID-19 associated mortality correlates with lowered [albumin] <30 mg/ml (Violi et al., 2020).
evidence: Established clinical reference range.

claim: COVID-19 associated mortality correlates with lowered albumin concentration <30 mg/ml.
source: The reference range of HSA concentration in serum is approximately 35–50 mg/ml, but we and other groups found that COVID-19 associated mortality correlates with lowered [albumin] <30 mg/ml (Violi et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from Violi et al., 2020 and confirmed by current study data.

claim: The order parameter S was consistently lower in Sev-R and further decreased in Sev-D patients relative to the control group, independent of the spin probe used.
source: However, independent of the spin probe and both in plasma and whole blood samples, the order parameter has been consistently lower in Sev-R which was further decreased in Sev-D patients relative to the control group (Figure 4D).
evidence: EPR spectroscopy measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Rotational mobility of 16-DSA (τc) was significantly faster when bound with HSA from COVID-19 patients relative to control subjects in plasma or whole blood.
source: Calculations of τc as described in Materials and methods showed rotational mobility of 16-DSA is significantly faster when bound with HSA from COVID-19 patients relative to that from control subjects in plasma or whole blood.
evidence: EPR spectroscopy measurements with calculated rotational correlation times.

claim: The HSA of COVID-19 patients is generally less water accessible relative to control subjects.
source: It is clear from these data that the HSA of COVID-19 patients is generally less water accessible relative to control ones.
evidence: Ascorbate reduction kinetics experiments shown in Figure 4G-J.

claim: The core of the HSA of both COVID-19 groups was not significantly different in terms of water accessibility.
source: However, the core of the HSA of both COVID-19 groups was not significantly different in terms of water accessibility.
evidence: Ascorbate reduction kinetics experiments.

claim: Fatty acid uptake by HSA is hindered in critically ill COVID-19 patients relative to controls.
source: These results (n=3) demonstrate the hindered fatty acid uptake by HSA of critically ill patients relative to controls.
evidence: Loading kinetics experiments shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Fatty acid redistribution upon ethanol addition is remarkably pronounced in critically ill patients, reflecting weaker association with and easier release of fatty acids from HSA.
source: Redistributions of the fatty acid populations are noticeable through decreased S and increased W (includes signals of free fatty acid) peaks. This redistribution is remarkably pronounced in critically ill patients reflecting weaker association with, and easier release of fatty acids from HSA in those patients.
evidence: Ethanol-induced unloading experiments shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: EPR-calculated parameters showed moderate-to-strong negative correlations with plasma H2O2 concentration (Pearson's r=–0.6 to –0.78, p<0.01 for all correlations).
source: Despite relatively small numbers of subjects analyzed, correlations of biophysical parameters showed moderate-to-strong negative correlations with [H2O2] in plasma or with DCF positive populations (% of total); Pearson's r=–0.6 to –0.78, p<0.01 for all correlations.
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: EPR-calculated parameters showed moderate-to-strong negative correlations with DCF positive neutrophil populations (Pearson's r=–0.6 to –0.78, p<0.01 for all correlations).
source: Despite relatively small numbers of subjects analyzed, correlations of biophysical parameters showed moderate-to-strong negative correlations with [H2O2] in plasma or with DCF positive populations (% of total); Pearson's r=–0.6 to –0.78, p<0.01 for all correlations.
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: Neutrophil-mediated oxidative stress in critically ill COVID-19 patients is a pivotal contributor to the observed structural changes in HSA.
source: These observations may suggest that neutrophil-mediated oxidative stress in critically ill COVID-19 patients is a pivotal contributor to the observed structural changes in HSA of those patients.
evidence: Inferred from correlation analyses between oxidative stress measures and HSA structural parameters.

claim: Patients with S/W ratio ≤0.15 showed significantly higher in-hospital mortality (81.8% vs. 18.2%, log-rank χ2=5.1, p=0.024).
source: Patients with lower values of the S/W ratio showed significantly higher in-hospital mortality (81.8% vs. 18.2%, log-rank χ2=5.1, p=0.024, Figure 6G).
evidence: Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Patients with plasma H2O2 above the mean showed higher mortality (65.2% vs. 34.8%, log-rank χ2=4.1, p=0.043).
source: Similarly, patients with accumulated H2O2 in their plasma showed higher mortality (65.2% vs. 34.8%, log-rank χ2=4.1, p=0.043, Figure 6H).
evidence: Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Risk score ((S/W)/[H2O2]) lower than 0.019 predicted mortality with excellent accuracy (95.5% vs. 4.5%, log-rank χ2=12.1, p=5×10–4).
source: However, when we combined these two parameters to derive a risk score as the ratio ((S/W)/[H2O2]), the resultant risk score lower than the mean (<0.019) predicted mortality with excellent accuracy (95.5% vs. 4.5%, log-rank χ2=12.1, p=5×10–4, Figure 6I).
evidence: Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Albumin level in plasma predicted mortality with acceptable accuracy (65.2% vs. 34.8%, log-rank χ2=6.85, p=0.009).
source: Finally, albumin level in plasma was found to predict mortality with acceptable accuracy (65.2% vs. 34.8%, log-rank χ2=6.85, p=0.009, Figure 6J).
evidence: Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 6J.

claim: HSA acts as an anti-inflammatory and antioxidant protein.
source: Closer to the context of COVID-19 pathophysiology, critical roles of HSA have been suggested as it acts as an anti-inflammatory and antioxidant protein (Inoue et al., 2018), anticoagulant agent (Doweiko and Nompleggi, 1991; Ronit et al., 2020), inhibitor of oxidative stress-mediated clotting and platelet activation (Basili et al., 2019; Tian et al., 2020), drug-dependent allosteric carrier and regulator (Fanali et al., 2012), and a potent heme scavenger that may also exhibit globin-like reactivity (Ascenzi et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Inoue et al., 2018.

claim: HSA acts as an anticoagulant agent.
source: Closer to the context of COVID-19 pathophysiology, critical roles of HSA have been suggested as it acts as an anti-inflammatory and antioxidant protein (Inoue et al., 2018), anticoagulant agent (Doweiko and Nompleggi, 1991; Ronit et al., 2020), inhibitor of oxidative stress-mediated clotting and platelet activation (Basili et al., 2019; Tian et al., 2020), drug-dependent allosteric carrier and regulator (Fanali et al., 2012), and a potent heme scavenger that may also exhibit globin-like reactivity (Ascenzi et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Doweiko and Nompleggi, 1991 and Ronit et al., 2020.

claim: HSA acts as an inhibitor of oxidative stress-mediated clotting and platelet activation.
source: Closer to the context of COVID-19 pathophysiology, critical roles of HSA have been suggested as it acts as an anti-inflammatory and antioxidant protein (Inoue et al., 2018), anticoagulant agent (Doweiko and Nompleggi, 1991; Ronit et al., 2020), inhibitor of oxidative stress-mediated clotting and platelet activation (Basili et al., 2019; Tian et al., 2020), drug-dependent allosteric carrier and regulator (Fanali et al., 2012), and a potent heme scavenger that may also exhibit globin-like reactivity (Ascenzi et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Basili et al., 2019 and Tian et al., 2020.

claim: HSA acts as a drug-dependent allosteric carrier and regulator.
source: Closer to the context of COVID-19 pathophysiology, critical roles of HSA have been suggested as it acts as an anti-inflammatory and antioxidant protein (Inoue et al., 2018), anticoagulant agent (Doweiko and Nompleggi, 1991; Ronit et al., 2020), inhibitor of oxidative stress-mediated clotting and platelet activation (Basili et al., 2019; Tian et al., 2020), drug-dependent allosteric carrier and regulator (Fanali et al., 2012), and a potent heme scavenger that may also exhibit globin-like reactivity (Ascenzi et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Fanali et al., 2012.

claim: HSA is a potent heme scavenger that may also exhibit globin-like reactivity.
source: Closer to the context of COVID-19 pathophysiology, critical roles of HSA have been suggested as it acts as an anti-inflammatory and antioxidant protein (Inoue et al., 2018), anticoagulant agent (Doweiko and Nompleggi, 1991; Ronit et al., 2020), inhibitor of oxidative stress-mediated clotting and platelet activation (Basili et al., 2019; Tian et al., 2020), drug-dependent allosteric carrier and regulator (Fanali et al., 2012), and a potent heme scavenger that may also exhibit globin-like reactivity (Ascenzi et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Ascenzi et al., 2015.

claim: Albumin acts as a frontline protection against COVID-19-associated lethality resulting from cytokine storm, oxidative stress, blood clotting, and organ failure.
source: In the light of these established functions, it is natural to suggest albumin as a frontline protection against COVID-19-associated lethality resulting from cytokine storm, oxidative stress, blood clotting, and the ensuing organ failure.
evidence: Inferred from established HSA functions and COVID-19 pathophysiology.

claim: Hypoalbuminemia has been repeatedly reported as a predictor of mortality in COVID-19.
source: Although hypoalbuminemia has been repeatedly reported as a predictor of mortality in COVID-19 (Violi et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2020), low albumin levels may result from surgery, dialysis, abdominal infections, liver failure, pancreatitis, respiratory distress, bypass surgery, ovarian problems caused by fertility drugs, and many other conditions.
evidence: Cited from Violi et al., 2020 and Huang et al., 2020.

claim: The study was designed to explore how COVID-19-caused mortality is related to oxidative stress and whether ROS-induced albumin damage can predict such outcome.
source: We designed the present study to explore how COVID-19-caused mortality is related to oxidative stress and whether ROS-induced albumin damage can be used to predict such outcome.
evidence: Stated study objective.

claim: The study recruited subjects from a homogeneous cohort in terms of disease severity, hospitalization, and interventions.
source: To avoid disparities related to clinical statuses and interventional protocols we restricted our subject recruitment to a homogeneous cohort of patients in terms of diseases severity, hospitalization, and interventions.
evidence: Study design description.

claim: Both sexes were represented in the overall COVID-19 subjects (40% females).
source: Both sexes were represented in the overal COVID-19 subjects (40% females) and sex was not found to affect mortality.
evidence: Demographic data from the study cohort.

claim: Sex was not found to affect mortality in the studied COVID-19 cohort.
source: Both sexes were represented in the overal COVID-19 subjects (40% females) and sex was not found to affect mortality.
evidence: Statistical analysis of demographic factors.

claim: The mean age of the studied subjects was 66.7±8.9 years (range 42–81).
source: The mean age of the studied subjects was 66.7±8.9 years (42–81), and non-survivors were slightly orlder.
evidence: Demographic data from the study cohort.

claim: Non-survivors were slightly older than survivors.
source: The mean age of the studied subjects was 66.7±8.9 years (42–81), and non-survivors were slightly orlder.
evidence: Demographic comparison between survivor and non-survivor groups.

claim: Impairment of HSA ability to transport ligands may affect the bioavailability of administered drugs.
source: For instance, impairment of HSA ability to transport an extremely wide range of endogenous and exogenous ligands may affect the bioavailability of adminsitered drugs (Lee and Wu, 2015), distribution of anti-inflammatory molecules such as NO and prostaglandins (Arroyo et al., 2014), as well as affecting its anticoagulation and antiplatelet activation functions (Paar et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Lee and Wu, 2015.

claim: Impairment of HSA ability to transport ligands may affect distribution of anti-inflammatory molecules such as NO and prostaglandins.
source: For instance, impairment of HSA ability to transport an extremely wide range of endogenous and exogenous ligands may affect the bioavailability of adminsitered drugs (Lee and Wu, 2015), distribution of anti-inflammatory molecules such as NO and prostaglandins (Arroyo et al., 2014), as well as affecting its anticoagulation and antiplatelet activation functions (Paar et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Arroyo et al., 2014.

claim: Impairment of HSA may affect its anticoagulation and antiplatelet activation functions.
source: For instance, impairment of HSA ability to transport an extremely wide range of endogenous and exogenous ligands may affect the bioavailability of adminsitered drugs (Lee and Wu, 2015), distribution of anti-inflammatory molecules such as NO and prostaglandins (Arroyo et al., 2014), as well as affecting its anticoagulation and antiplatelet activation functions (Paar et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Paar et al., 2017.

claim: Reduced and damaged HSA may disturb the vascular oncotic pressure contributing to pulmonary edema and gastrointestinal symptoms.
source: Reduced and damaged HSA may also disturb the vascular oncotic pressure contributing to pulmonary edema and potentially to gastrointestinal symptoms that characterize recent waves of the infection.
evidence: Inferred from HSA's role in maintaining oncotic pressure and observed COVID-19 symptoms.

claim: Albumin-related changes are more robust predictors of mortality and severity than immune-related parameters such as cytokine levels, CRP, and D-dimer.
source: We believe that the current data suggest that albumin-related changes are more robust predictors of mortality and severity than immune-related parameters, such as cytokine levels, CRP, D-dimer, and so on.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of statistical significance of different parameters in predicting mortality.

claim: The identified parameters can be used as accurate mortality predictors of critically ill COVID-19 patients.
source: Our current findings substantiate the utilization of the identified parameters as accurate mortality predictors of critically ill COVID-19 patients.
evidence: Based on survival analysis results showing strong predictive power.

claim: Determining threshold values of these parameters can help identify patients in need of urgent medical attention.
source: Determining threshold values of these parameters can possibly help to identify patients in need of urgent medical attention, and may provide novel markers to assess new candidates for COVID-19 treatments targeting HSA replacements.
evidence: Inferred from the predictive power of the identified parameters.

claim: The identified parameters may provide novel markers to assess new candidates for COVID-19 treatments targeting HSA replacements.
source: Determining threshold values of these parameters can possibly help to identify patients in need of urgent medical attention, and may provide novel markers to assess new candidates for COVID-19 treatments targeting HSA replacements.
evidence: Inferred from the mechanistic link between HSA damage and mortality.

claim: The study suggests the importance of studying the potential effects of albumin replacement therapy on clinical outcomes of COVID-19 patients.
source: We thus suggest the importance of studying the potential effects of albumin replacement therapy on clinical outcomes of Covid-19 patients.
evidence: Recommendation based on findings linking HSA damage to mortality.

claim: The results provide new mechanistic insights into pathways that could be targeted to help prevent critical COVID illness and death, for example, oxidative stress.
source: Our results also provide new mechanistic insights into pathways that could be targeted to help prevent critical COVID illness and death, for example, oxidative stress.
evidence: Based on the demonstrated link between oxidative stress and mortality.

claim: All patients were recruited from Kasr Alainy Cairo University Hospital/ICU-facility at the Internal Medicine Quarantine Hospital.
source: All patients were recruited from Kasr Alainy Cairo University Hospital/ICU-facility at the Internal Medicine Quarantine Hospital.
evidence: Study design and recruitment information.

claim: Patients recruited in the current study were divided into two arms based on future mortality outcome: survivors (Sev-R) and deceased (Sev-D).
source: Patients recruited in the current study were divided into two arms based on future mortality outcome: those who survived the past 15 days following blood samples collection (Sev-R) and those who died within 15 days of samples collection (Sev-D).
evidence: Study design description.

claim: Sample collection continued until a total of N=40 was reached for COVID-19 patients diagnosed as severely infected with SARS-CoV-2 and admitted to the ICU during October 13, 2020 to February 21, 2021.
source: Sample size was based on sample availability and collection continued until a total of N=40 has been reached (39 samples analyzed in the current study) for COVID-19 patients diagnosed as severely infected with SARS-CoV-2 and admitted to the ICU during the period from October 13, 2020 to February 21, 2021.
evidence: Study design and recruitment timeline.

claim: Within the follow-up time, 23 patients had died.
source: Within the follow-up time, 23 patients had died.
evidence: Study outcome data.

claim: All available 39 samples were investigated by blinded operators and were all included in the final analysis.
source: Nevertheless, all available 39 samples were investigated by blinded operators and were all included in the final analysis.
evidence: Study methodology description.

claim: Analysis of fresh samples precluded operators' bias as the censored outcome is a future event.
source: Analysis of fresh samples precluded operators' bias as the censored outcome is a future event.
evidence: Study methodology description addressing potential bias.

claim: Patients who survived 15 days post sample collections were considered survivors (Sev-R).
source: Patients who survived 15 days post sample collections were considered survivors (Sev-R) while those who died within this period were placed in the Sev-D group.
evidence: Study classification criteria.

source: Patients who survived 15 days post sample collections were considered survivors (Sev-R) while those who died within this period were placed in the Sev-D group.

source: Written informed consents were obtained from all participants in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.

source: For COVID-19 and control blood/plasma collection, Children's Cancer Hospital's Institutional Review Board (IRB) has evaluated the study design and protocol, IRB number 31-2020 issued on July 6, 2020.
evidence: Ethical approval documentation.

claim: EPR spectra were measured at 37°C using a Benchtop Magnettech MiniScope MS5000 spectrometer.
source: We measured EPR spectra at 37°C using a Benchtop Magnettech MiniScope MS5000 spectrometer (now Bruker Biospin, Berlin) equipped with biotemperature control and computerized data acquisition and analysis capabilities.
evidence: Methodological description of EPR measurements.

claim: Typical EPR instrumental parameters were: microwave frequency 9.47 GHz, microwave power 10 mW, modulation frequency 100 kHz, modulation amplitude 0.2 mT, and magnetic field range 332–342 mT.
source: Typical instrumental parameters during these measurements were: microwave frequency 9.47 GHz, microwave power 10 mW, modulation frequency 100 kHz, modulation amplitude 0.2 mT, and magnetic field range 332–342 mT.
evidence: Methodological description of EPR measurement parameters.

claim: Each EPR spectrum was the average of 5 scans with scan time of 60 s.
source: Each spectrum was the average of 5 scans with scan time of 60 s.
evidence: Methodological description of EPR data acquisition.

claim: Hypoalbuminemia is suggested as a pivotal marker for the pathology of many infections.
source: Although hypoalbuminemia is suggested as a pivotal marker for the pathology of many infections (reviewed very recently in Wiedermann, 2021) including in COVID-19 (Violi et al., 2020), albumin damage has not been directly implicated in infectious disease to the best of our knowledge.
evidence: Cited from a review by Wiedermann, 2021.

claim: Albumin damage has not been directly implicated in infectious disease prior to this study.
source: Although hypoalbuminemia is suggested as a pivotal marker for the pathology of many infections (reviewed very recently in Wiedermann, 2021) including in COVID-19 (Violi et al., 2020), albumin damage has not been directly implicated in infectious disease to the best of our knowledge.
evidence: Statement about novelty of the current findings.
